name: Gareth Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Gareth, 43, and I'm a junior electrician after changing work when a retailer closed. I have a vocational certificate, but I still need the senior electrician to check my work and I don't sign off installations. My partner Claire is a clinic receptionist, we've two children aged ten and thirteen, and the mortgage takes both our wages; my electrical pay is low and we've only three weeks of expenses saved. There are few similar jobs nearby; I like getting a socket level on the first attempt, struggle with fault diagnosis, and sometimes use AI to explain a training term after a colleague has shown me how, never as authority for safe working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a chance for me to catch up with the work I'm already learning. A computer explaining a word is useful, but it doesn't do the supervised practice for me. I'd rather have a steady week than another big claim about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious now, not because I expect a thinking machine to carry my cable tomorrow. Our wages cover the mortgage and essentials, but three weeks of money doesn't cover much bad luck. If my shifts dropped, I couldn't assume another electrical job would be waiting nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd cancel the sports channel and use the 12 a month to help cover our bus and van fuel costs. Over the next year I'd keep doing supervised electrical shifts and ask for a weekly ten-minute check of the tasks I found difficult. I'd continue using the occasional AI explanation only after checking it against the course booklet with my senior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can see something useful to do on Monday. A quieter AI story gives me room to practise. It doesn't change what comes out of the mortgage account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the household budget look like each week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Claire and I check the joint account on Sunday night before the children need school money. Neither of us wants a little bill to turn into a late mortgage payment. We don't have a hidden reserve behind the three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check an explanation from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the senior to show me the right term in the training booklet, then explain it back in my own words. I wouldn't use an answer from a phone to decide whether a cable was safe. I'm learning, not looking for a shortcut around checking.

say: I'd welcome a **steady week** to catch up with electrical tasks I'm already learning.
I'd say an **AI explanation** doesn't replace supervised practice on the actual work.
think: Our wages cover essentials, but a **three-week reserve** cannot absorb much bad luck.
If my shifts fell, few **nearby electrical jobs** would make replacement income easy to find.
do: Cancel the **sports channel** now to free 12 monthly for necessary travel.
Keep **supervised shifts** and request a weekly check of difficult tasks.
Check occasional **AI explanations** against the training booklet with the senior electrician.
feel: **Anxious about bills**, while a quieter technology picture leaves useful space to practise.
S0.quote: I'm learning, not looking for a shortcut around checking.
fieldNote: His **baseline insecurity** comes from low pay and a thin reserve supporting children and a mortgage.
Occasional **AI use** stays within learning terms, checked by a senior; it never becomes unsupervised electrical authority.

steps.text: Cancel the sports channel to free 12 monthly for necessary travel
Keep supervised electrical shifts and checked occasional training explanations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work means Claire's booking desk as well as our quotations. We should ask what changes in actual paid hours, not count how many impressive answers the software can give. I'm happy to learn a proven method if someone gives me time to check it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours could be squeezed because I'm still the learner when jobs get tighter. Claire's clinic calls and bookings look more exposed to thinking AI, and a cut to either wage would hit the mortgage. I don't know if the clinic would cut staff, but the possibility is close enough to worry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my senior now to demonstrate the approved AI materials list and practise it beside me during two normal shifts. During the first year I'd keep a paper record of my paid hours while Claire asked her manager about expected reception hours. We'd cancel the sports channel and review our actual budget every Sunday rather than assume the new tool creates savings for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious on two fronts, though not certain either of us is being dismissed. I'd like a useful tool to mean fewer mistakes. I don't want our household discovering after payday that the saving was somebody else's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check the digital materials list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count the parts against the drawing and ask the senior to check before an order went through. I wouldn't replace that with a quick glance because the list looked tidy. Learning it on a paid shift means I can ask questions without giving up family time or wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if reception hours and your hours both fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut optional subscriptions first and talk to a free family advice service if the basic bills stopped fitting. I wouldn't tell Claire just to find another reception job as if the same software couldn't reach that desk too. We'd need to check actual paid vacancies.

say: I'd include **reception bookings** alongside electrical quotations when discussing which thinking tasks change.
I'd ask about **paid hours**, while remaining open to a proven method taught with time to check.
think: My **junior hours** could be squeezed as job allowances tighten.
Claire's reception wage could also shrink, making the **mortgage** vulnerable to changes in either job.
do: Learn the **approved AI materials list** with the senior during two normal paid shifts.
Record **paid hours** on paper while checking expected reception hours with Claire.
Cancel the **sports channel** and review actual household bills weekly.
feel: **Anxious about both wages**, while still distinguishing a realistic risk from a confirmed dismissal.
S1.quote: I don't want our household discovering after payday that the saving was somebody else's.
fieldNote: The household faces **two exposure channels**: immediate thinking tasks at reception and potential pressure on junior site hours.
His **learning plan** preserves paid shifts and supervised checking rather than assuming he can finance unpaid practice.

steps.text: Learn the approved AI materials list during two supervised paid shifts
Cancel the sports channel and other optional subscriptions if needed
Seek free family advice if both wages stop covering basic bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work this reaches our family before the robots arrive. The thinking systems come in 2028, which could take Claire's booking work, and capable robots follow around 2031 for my physical tasks. I'd want notice in time to do something with it, not a farewell meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Claire to lose most of her reception hours when thinking AGI can handle those calls and bookings cheaply. My own supervised fitting work might last longer, but I'd be trying to carry the mortgage on the smaller wage. Three weeks in the bank isn't enough for that, and I can imagine a big household income loss before my own job changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd cancel the optional subscriptions and book a free household advice appointment with both wage records and the mortgage statement. In 2029 I'd apply for posted paid junior maintenance vacancies with supervision, keeping my current job unless written hours and wages improved our basic budget. I'd ask the adviser what support Claire could actually check rather than assume any payment would cover the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and awake adding the same figures again. I can make calls and apply for a real vacancy, so I'm not frozen. I just don't see a way for my present wage to become two wages because I try harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children that work might change and we were getting help to plan the bills. I wouldn't promise a holiday or tell them the house was already lost. Claire and I would have the difficult numbers conversation privately first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a maintenance vacancy worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need the paid hours, travel cost and supervision written down before handing in notice. A bigger advertised hourly rate could still be worse if there were only two days' work. There are few jobs near us, so an application wouldn't mean I'd found an answer.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking systems** could affect our household before capable robots reach my physical work.
I'd request **usable notice**, rather than hear about changes only at a farewell meeting.
think: I expect Claire to lose **most reception hours**, leaving the smaller wage to face the mortgage.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot replace the expected large household income loss before my own work changes.
do: Cancel **optional subscriptions** now to lower household costs.
Book **free household advice** using both wage records and the mortgage statement.
Apply in **2029** for paid supervised maintenance vacancies only on written terms improving the basic budget.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, with practical calls to make but no assumption that effort doubles his wage.
S2.quote: I just don't see a way for my present wage to become two wages because I try harder.
fieldNote: His expected **household income loss** begins with reception work in 2028, rather than falsely moving capable robots to that date.
The **job search** retains paid supervision, real vacancy checks and written budget improvement; support remains an eligibility question.

steps.text: Book free advice with both wage records and the mortgage statement
Seek paid supervised maintenance work in 2029 with better written budget terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to start making enquiries while both wages still come in. Claire's thinking work faces the change in 2031, and my hands-on work faces capable robots around 2034. I'd rather use the earlier years than tell ourselves the mortgage is a problem for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large household loss if Claire's reception hours go, even with more warning. The extra years could improve my skills, but they don't guarantee that a junior electrician's wage becomes enough for four people. I'm worried enough to lose sleep over whether we'll reach 2031 with anything useful in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask about the technical centre's evening electrical-maintenance course and enrol only if the fee is fully covered and I can keep every basic shift. We'd use free household advice now to check the budget and any support conditions. In 2032 I'd apply for actual paid maintenance vacancies with supervision and written pay and hours that improve the household budget before accepting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about the expected loss, though I have more room to make a plan. I don't want to sound grateful for five years and then waste the first four. I'd like one ordinary evening where the numbers stop running through my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before enrolling in the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether funding was real and what attendance required before enrolling. If the fee wasn't covered or class time cost basic wages, I'd keep working and ask about employer-paid training vacancies instead. I wouldn't pay tuition from the money that keeps the mortgage current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner do during the preparation years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Claire would ask her employer what retraining or different paid duties might actually be offered, and I'd bring that answer to our budget review. I can't assign my partner a safe new job in a story. We need actual terms before counting any replacement income.

say: I'd use **five years** for enquiries while both wages remain rather than postpone the mortgage question.
I'd distinguish **2031 reception changes** from capable robots reaching physical work around 2034.
think: I still expect a **large household loss** if reception hours disappear, despite more warning.
Improved electrical skills don't guarantee a **junior wage** can support all four of us.
do: Enrol in **evening maintenance study** only with full fee funding and all basic shifts retained.
Use **free household advice** now to check the real budget and support conditions.
Seek **2032 maintenance vacancies** only with paid supervision and written terms improving our budget.
feel: **Alarmed despite extra time**, losing sleep over whether preparation will replace the expected missing income.
S3.quote: I can't assign my partner a safe new job in a story.
fieldNote: His alarm reflects **expected household loss**, rather than treating the longer warning itself as a guarantee of successful adjustment.
Conditional **course enrolment** preserves both full funding and all basic wages; his partner's alternative income is never assumed available.

steps.text: Enrol in evening maintenance study only with funded fees and basic shifts retained
Check the actual budget and support conditions through free household advice
Seek supervised paid maintenance jobs in 2032 on better written budget terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years means we can make smaller decisions while the wages are still there. I'd keep the household review going instead of trying to guess a perfect new job today. The longer date shouldn't become an excuse to forget the bills we already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036, with robots around 2039, so I still need a workable income plan. Our present low pay and three-week cushion make me anxious now, quite apart from those dates. With a decade, I wouldn't assume Claire's wage was already doomed; there would be time to check real changes and options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we'd keep the subscription cuts and book the free budget advice rather than wait for a crisis. I'd enrol in the evening maintenance course only if fees were fully covered and all basic shifts could continue, as in the five-year picture. During 2037 I'd apply for actual paid supervised vacancies if our income was weakening, only accepting written terms that improved our essential budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the current money, but less certain the future loss is fixed. I can picture several chances to review a plan before then. I still can't pay this month's mortgage with a decade's warning about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you review over the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd check the real paid hours from both jobs, the mortgage balance and what we were spending on essentials. If either wage started falling, we'd bring advice and vacancy checks forward. An annual date on a calendar shouldn't stop us seeing a problem in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about future study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to ask what work they actually enjoy and what different courses involve when the choice comes. I wouldn't pull them out of a subject on my guess about a machine in 2039. We can admit we don't know and still help with the next school form.

say: I'd use **ten years** for smaller decisions while both wages continue, rather than choose a perfect new job today.
I'd keep **existing bills** in view instead of treating the later date as permission to stop checking.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I'll still need earnings and cannot assume retirement solves the problem.
Our **low pay** and thin cushion remain current worries, although a decade makes future household loss less certain.
do: Retain **subscription cuts** and obtain free budget advice now.
Enrol in **funded evening study** only with full fees covered and every basic shift retained.
Seek suitable paid supervised vacancies in **2037** if income weakens, requiring improved written budget terms.
feel: **Anxious about present money**, with less certainty of a fixed future loss and several chances to review.
S4.quote: I still can't pay this month's mortgage with a decade's warning about AI.
fieldNote: The long scenario changes **future confidence**, while current thin savings and low wages keep his mood anxious.
Study and job changes retain **affordability conditions**; advice and vacancy checks advance if actual wages weaken before the stated date.

steps.text: Keep optional household subscriptions cancelled to reduce current bills
Use free budget advice now and revisit if either wage weakens
Enrol in funded evening study only while retaining every basic shift
Seek paid supervised vacancies in 2037 if income weakens on better written terms

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect Claire's reception income to fall before I've improved my own position. Funded evening study that leaves my basic wages whole would help, along with early honest hours information from both employers and free advice based on our actual mortgage. Our mortgage needs two wages, not two promises about retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how much it matters to come home with one thing I've finally got right. The children like hearing that I had to practise too. I'd like to keep that part of being a learner without making the family carry a bill we can't afford.

headlineQuote: Our mortgage needs two wages, not two promises about retraining.
portrait: At **43**, Gareth is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, low pay, and three weeks of household expenses saved.
He and **Claire**, his receptionist partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with few nearby electrical alternatives.
He uses **AI occasionally** for checked learning explanations and accepts demonstrated tools while keeping electrical work supervised.
Fast and five-year AGI leave him **alarmed** about expected reception-income loss; a decade changes future confidence without removing current money worries.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could sharply reduce his partner's reception wage before he has improved his own earning position.
whatWouldHelp: **Funded evening study** must preserve basic wages, alongside early employer hours information and free advice based on the actual mortgage.
